quote.p: He begins his history with Aeneas, son of Anchises, son of Capys, who flourished during the Trojan War, fled after the capture of Troy, and after long wandering sailed to a shore of Italy called Laurentum, where his camp is still shown, and from him they call the coast Troy. At that time Faunus, son of Ares, ruled over the Aborigines, the Italians of that region; he gave his daughter Lavinia in marriage to Aeneas along with a territory of four hundred stades in circuit. Aeneas founded a city and named it Lavinium after his wife. When Faunus died in the third year, Aeneas succeeded to the rule by virtue of his marriage alliance and named the Aborigines "Latins" after his father-in-law Latinus Faunus. Three years later again, on account of his wife Lavinia—who had previously been betrothed to their king—Aeneas was killed in war by the Rutulians, a Tyrrhenian people, and Euryleon, renamed Ascanius, succeeded to the rule; he had been born to Aeneas by Creusa, daughter of Priam, who had been his wife at Troy. Others, however, say that Ascanius, his successor to the rule, was born to him by Lavinia.

When Ascanius died in the fourth year after the founding of Alba (for he too founded a city, calling it Alba, and moved the people from Lavinium), Silvius succeeded to the rule. They say that Silvius's son was Aeneas Silvius, Aeneas's was Latinus Silvius, his was Capys, Capys's was Capetus, Capetus's was Tiberinus, his was Agrippa, and his was Romulus—who was struck by a thunderbolt; his son was Aventinus, and Aventinus's was Procas. All of them bore the surname Silvius. To Procas were born two sons, the elder Numitor and the younger Amulius. When the elder received the rule from his dying father, the younger seized and held it by arrogance and force. He killed his brother's son Egestus and appointed his daughter Rhea Silvia a priestess so that she might remain childless; Numitor himself was saved from plots against his life by the gentleness of his character and his great mildness. Yet Silvia conceived contrary to the law. Amulius arrested her for punishment, and handed the two children born to her over to shepherds to cast the infants into the nearby river; Tiber was the name of the river, and Romus and Romulus were the children, tracing their lineage from Aeneas on their mother's side—for their father's lineage is uncertain.

The first book contains the deeds and achievements of the seven kings: Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Ancus Hostilius, another Ancus also called Marcius (a descendant of Numa), Tarquinius, Servius Tullius, and Lucius Tarquinius, son of Tarquinius. The first of these, who had been the founder and builder of Rome and had ruled more like a father than a tyrant, was nonetheless murdered—or, as others say, vanished. The second, having reigned no less well, if not even better, ended his life after living The third was struck by a thunderbolt. The fourth departed life by disease. The fifth was murdered by shepherds, and the sixth likewise ended his life by murder. The seventh was driven out of both the city and the kingship for his lawlessness; from that time the kingship was abolished and the government was transferred to the consuls.

At Tatius's command they pelted the girl with their gold until, wounded, she was buried beneath it.

The war of Tatius against Romulus was arbitrated by the wives of the Romans and daughters of the Sabines, who went in person to their parents' camp, stretching out their hands, holding up the infants already born to them by their husbands, and testifying that their husbands had done them no outrage. They begged the Sabines to take pity on themselves, their kinsmen by marriage, their grandchildren, and their daughters, and to abstain from a wicked war among kin—or else to kill them first, who were the cause of the war. The Sabines, both from the difficulty of their situation and from pity for the women, realizing now that the Romans had done this not out of insolence but out of necessity, yielded to reconciliation. Romulus and Tatius met on the road that from then on became the Sacred Way and agreed on these terms: that both Tatius and Romulus should reign jointly, and that the Sabines who had then marched with Tatius, along with any other Sabines who wished, should settle in the Roman state on equal and fair terms.

The consuls held up the oaths and declared they would yield to anything rather than admit Tarquinius.

Tarquinius was stirring up the Sabines against the Romans. But Claudius, an influential Sabine from the city of Regillus, tried to prevent the Sabines from breaking the treaty, until, put on trial for this, he fled to Rome with five thousand kinsmen, friends, and slaves. To all of these the Romans gave space for houses and land for farming, and made them citizens; Claudius himself they even enrolled in the Senate, as he performed brilliant deeds against the Sabines, and they established a tribe named after him.
